ABLS: Small US companies chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital invested in the business, spread across health care, finance, technology and industry. It is a quality-focused way to own small caps, which swing more than big-company stocks, with a screen meant to skip the weakest balance sheets.
AINF: Companies making the chips that run artificial intelligence models after they are trained, the inference stage where AI answers questions in data centers and devices. It is a narrow bet on one stage of the AI buildout, separate from the firms that design the biggest training processors.
AIX: One hundred US companies picked for having an AI moat, meaning a position in artificial intelligence that rivals would find hard to copy. Technology is about seven-tenths of the fund, so it is a growth bet on AI winners that swings more than the broad market.
AT: The muscles of robots: makers of actuators, motors and precision motion parts, mostly Japanese and US industrial companies, that let machines move. It is a narrow slice of the robotics industry rather than the whole field, so it lives or dies on factory automation spending.
AV: Aerospace and aviation companies: aircraft and engine makers, defense contractors and the suppliers behind commercial flight, all in the industrial sector. It is a focused bet on air travel and military spending, so it moves with airline orders and defense budgets rather than the broad economy.
BBYY: An income fund built on options tied to a fund holding Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce giant, rather than owning those shares directly. It aims to pay frequent distributions, and what sets it apart is the China link: Alibaba's price swings with Chinese consumer spending and Beijing's rules for tech companies.
BFAP: Options-based exposure to bitcoin with a floor built in, designed so losses over its outcome period stop at a set level, the Floor15 in its name. This April series gives up some gains in exchange for that protection, so it is a cautious way to hold bitcoin rather than chasing its whole rise.
BLCK: The plumbing of crypto: exchanges, miners, custodians and trading platforms that make money from digital assets without the fund holding coins itself. Financial companies are more than four-fifths of the fund, and because their fortunes follow crypto prices, it swings nearly as hard as the coins do.
BOBP: Large US companies chosen by a rules-based system, tilted toward technology at about a third and industrial companies at close to another third. What sets it apart is flexibility: the strategy can move part of the fund into cash when conditions look risky, trading some upside for smaller drops.
BREW: Coffee and energy drink companies from across the business: growers, roasters, bottlers and cafe chains, with consumer staples at about three-fifths of the fund. It is a focused bet on caffeine habits, so it depends on drinks staying in daily routines rather than on the wider food industry.
CHIP: Chipmaking companies from across the supply chain, including the firms that design AI processors and the ones that build the equipment used to manufacture them. It is a focused bet on artificial intelligence hardware, so it swings more than the broad tech sector and depends on chip spending staying strong.
CHNL: Exposure to Chainlink, the network that feeds real-world data like prices into blockchains, gained through futures contracts rather than holding the token itself. Prices are set by speculators in the futures market, so the fund can drift from the token's spot price and swings hard either way.
CRAM: Chinese memory and storage chip companies listed in mainland China and Hong Kong, covering the firms that make the memory inside phones, computers and data centers. It is a narrow, single-country bet on a strategic industry, so it carries both sharp industry swings and the political risks of investing in China.
DOCK: Railroads, ports and freight companies: the infrastructure that moves goods across North America and through its harbors, almost entirely in the industrial sector. It is a bet on trade volumes and supply chains, so it tends to do well when the economy is shipping a lot of stuff.
EEE: A fixed blend in one fund: about three-quarters in the 500 biggest US companies across every industry, and about a quarter in Ethereum, the blockchain network behind most smart contracts. The stock side behaves like a core holding, while the Ethereum slice adds sharp swings that can dominate the fund's moves.
FINY: An income fund that sells put options on a leveraged fund of financial stocks, one that aims for three times the daily move of its index. It aims to pay weekly distributions from option premiums, but the leveraged link means sharp drops in bank stocks can hit it hard.
FIYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund of long-term US Treasury bonds, rather than on holding the bonds themselves. It aims to pay weekly distributions, but long-term bond prices swing hard when interest rates move, and the leveraged link magnifies that, so drops can be steep.
GARA: Real assets from around the world: infrastructure operators, utilities, property companies and data center owners whose value sits in physical things. It is built for income from toll-road-like businesses and rents, and what sets it apart is the global mix, so currency moves matter alongside the assets.
GSKH: Shares of one company, GSK, the British drugmaker, held through its US-listed depositary receipts rather than bought directly in London. Like others in this series, it is built to soften the effect of currency moves between the pound and the dollar, leaving the stock itself as the main driver.
HBTC: Exposure to bitcoin with a built-in hedge, meaning part of the fund is positioned to soften the drop when bitcoin falls sharply. Bitcoin is famously volatile, so the trade-off here is giving up some of the upside in rallies in exchange for a less bruising ride.
HFSP: Large US stocks paired with cash, managed by trading models that shift between being invested and sitting in cash. The equity-hedged approach aims to blunt big market drops by pulling back, though that also means it can lag when stocks rally while the models are cautious.
HMYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund linked to Hims and Hers, the telehealth company, rather than owning the stock itself. It aims for frequent distributions, but the leveraged options structure swings sharply, so it fits short holding periods and speculation more than steady income investing.
HULL: Shipping lines, couriers and freight companies that move goods around the world, mostly industrial firms with a large slice of energy in the tanker trade. It is a bet on global trade and freight rates, so it does best when the world economy is moving a lot of cargo.
HYGM: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier kind that pay more interest, held through a big bond fund plus an options overlay that sells call options expiring weekly. It targets the income level in its name, and the trade-off is bond risk: these borrowers are the ones most likely to struggle in a downturn.
ICMO: Foreign stock markets chosen by momentum: the fund holds country funds from outside the US and rotates toward whichever national markets have been rising most. Because it chases strength country by country, its mix of regions changes over time, and it can zig when markets suddenly reverse.
LATR: Payment networks, digital wallets and checkout lenders: the companies behind buy now, pay later and other installment credit offered when shoppers pay. Financial companies are about two-thirds of the fund, so it is a focused bet on shoppers splitting purchases into payments instead of using traditional credit cards.
LCTO: Large US companies, reached mainly through a broad index fund, paired with municipal bonds and options in a structure designed to be tax-efficient. The idea is stock market growth with a smaller tax bill, so it fits taxable accounts, though the bond side can mute returns in strong rallies.
LFDR: Long-term US Treasury bonds, the safest borrowers in the market, held to pay a steady stream of income over many years. Because the bonds are long-term, the price moves a lot when interest rates change, even though the income itself is backed by the US government.
LPSV: Small and midsize US companies that look cheap relative to their earnings and assets, picked one by one by an active manager. It aims for the long-run payoff of value investing in smaller companies, which can mean years of lagging the big growth stocks before the style comes back.
MSR: A fund built on autocallable notes tied to MicroStrategy, the software company that has become a bitcoin proxy, using derivatives rather than the stock itself. Autocallables pay coupons and can be called away early when the stock cooperates, so the income comes with complicated, capped upside and real downside if the stock sinks.
MWHS: Electricity prices themselves, traded through futures contracts on power markets rather than shares of utility companies. Power prices spike with heat waves, cold snaps and grid strain, so this is a volatile trading tool whose moves have little to do with the stock market.
NYNY: Companies headquartered in or with major operations in New York City, led by big banks and financial firms at about two-thirds of the fund. It is a playful, concentrated bet on one city's economy, so it leans heavily on Wall Street's fortunes rather than spreading across the country.
OCT: A defined-outcome fund that follows US stocks through options, built to absorb a first slice of losses over its outcome period in exchange for capped gains. The October series runs on a yearly cycle that resets each fall, so the protection on offer depends on when in that cycle shares are bought.
ODDZ: Casinos, sportsbooks and online betting platforms: consumer companies built on gambling, from Las Vegas resorts to phone-based wagering apps. It is a focused bet on betting becoming a mainstream pastime, so it swings with consumer spending and with state-by-state legalization decisions.
QFHD: Dividend-paying companies from the 500 biggest US stocks, screened for strong free cash flow and quality, then weighted toward the highest yields. It is built for income with a quality filter, so it owns more banks, utilities and staples than the broad market and less fast-growing technology.
SAPH: Shares of one company, SAP, the German business software giant, bought through its US-listed depositary receipts. What sets it apart is a built-in currency hedge, which strips out most of the effect of euro moves against the dollar, so the fund rises and falls mostly with the stock itself.
SSS: A fixed blend in one fund: about three-quarters in the 500 biggest US companies across every industry, and about a quarter in Solana, a fast blockchain network's token. The stock side behaves like a core holding, while the Solana slice adds sharp swings that can dominate the fund's moves.
TMYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund holding Taiwan Semiconductor stock, the giant chipmaker, rather than on owning shares directly. It aims to pay out frequent distributions, but the leveraged link makes it swing hard, so it suits short holding periods rather than a set-and-forget core position.
TRUF: Financial companies across the industry: banks, insurers, payment networks and asset managers, actively picked rather than held in index weights. It is a focused bet on the financial system, so it does well when lending and markets are healthy and falls hard in banking scares.
TRUH: Health care companies of every kind: drugmakers, insurers, hospital operators and medical device firms, actively picked across the whole sector. It is a focused bet on medical spending, which tends to hold up in recessions, though drug pricing politics can hit parts of it hard.
TRUO: Consumer staples companies: the makers and sellers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products that people buy in any economy. It is a defensive holding, actively picked across the sector, and it usually falls less in downturns but grows more slowly in booms.
UPGR: Companies building green infrastructure: renewable power producers, clean technology manufacturers and the industrial firms installing them, picked against sustainability criteria. Industrials are about half the fund, so it is a focused bet on the energy transition, and it can lag badly when clean energy falls out of favor.
WATS: Companies that build battery storage systems, from home backup units to grid-scale installations that store solar and wind power for later use. It is a focused bet on batteries becoming part of the power grid, so it rides the fortunes of renewable energy and electric vehicles.
WNDR: Travel and leisure companies: airlines, hotels, theme parks, cruise and booking platforms, and the card networks travelers pay with. It is a focused bet on people spending on trips and experiences, so it falls hard when households cut back or travel is disrupted.
WR: Mostly energy companies, plus defense contractors and security technology firms, picked for their role in US defense and energy security. Energy is almost two-thirds of the fund, so it is a focused bet on conflict and defense spending rather than a broad market holding, and it rises and falls with oil prices.
WZRD: An actively traded fund where the manager moves between individual stocks, index funds and options or futures as opportunities appear, so its mix can change fast. Right now it leans toward technology, but nothing about the portfolio is fixed, making it a bet on the trader's timing calls.
XEY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund linked to ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, rather than holding ether itself. It aims to pay weekly distributions, but ether is volatile and the leveraged options link magnifies every swing, so it is a trading tool.
XXX: A fixed blend in one fund: about three-quarters in the 500 biggest US companies across every industry, and about a quarter in XRP, the token of a payments-focused blockchain network. The stock side behaves like a core holding, while the XRP slice adds sharp swings that can dominate the fund's moves.
ZCBF: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2034, bought at a discount and paying no interest along the way. It is built for a goal dated around 2034, and because nothing is paid until maturity, its price swings more than most bond funds when interest rates move.
ZCBG: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2035, bought at a discount and paying no interest along the way. It is built for a goal dated around 2035, and because nothing is paid until maturity, its price swings more than most bond funds when interest rates move.
